fullText:
One of the strangest limits of a Transformer is this:

It may reach the right interpretation in its deep layers—and still answer from an earlier, weaker one.

New paper:

RECIRCULATION

The motivating failure is wonderfully simple.

A model reads that Fred took a fishing pole to the bank. It correctly interprets “bank” as the edge of a river—then later says an ATM is likely to be there.

The knowledge was not absent.

The state did not circulate.

In a feedforward Transformer, understanding develops as representations move upward through the stack. Once a useful belief state emerges deep in the network, earlier layers cannot use it. Response generation can outrun semantic convergence.

Recirculation changes the geometry of inference.

At each input step, it sends a carefully scaled fraction of deep-layer activation back into a shallower layer. The model’s own contextualized state guides what happens next.

The frozen Transformer begins to behave like a dynamical system that can carry belief through time.

Not ordinary chain-of-thought.
Not standard depth looping.
Not recurrent pretraining from scratch.

Basic recirculation is training-free. Adaptive recirculation trains only a small token-conditioned mixing module while leaving the foundation model untouched.

On Gemma3, the reported gains are striking:

23% mean reduction in perplexity across nine datasets

GSM8K pass@1 rising from 29.3% to 35.5%—a 21% relative increase

Essentially no additional latency during token generation

The trade-off is serial prefill: long prompts take longer to ingest.

Why this matters:

We may be spending expensive chain-of-thought tokens on a problem that is partly architectural.

Complex inference deserves deliberate reasoning.

Basic state tracking should happen inside the machine.

This paper joins a broader 2026 shift toward temporal intelligence: Equilibrium Reasoners learn attractors; Language Models Need Sleep shifts compute into consolidation; T²MLR carries middle-layer state across steps.

A common frontier is emerging:

Intelligence is not only what a network stores.

It is how internal state evolves, returns, stabilizes and informs what comes next.

The authors are careful: this is not yet a universal production upgrade. Architecture compatibility and hyperparameters matter, and long-context prefill remains a real cost.

But the deeper contribution is profound:

A trained model may contain clues for how its own architecture should evolve.

Full credit to Michael C. Mozer, Shoaib Ahmed Siddiqui, Danny Sawyer, Sunny Sanyal and Rosanne Liu.

I’m attaching the first page because the abstract deserves a close reading.

Paper :
https://t.co/0kd1baTkVI

Perhaps the next leap will not come from giving models more thoughts to say.

It may come from allowing what they already understand to keep circulating.

fullText:
The most important agentic workflows are the ones where you collaborate with the agent, verify its results, and encode them as a skill or verifier for reuse. 

This works for things like writing, researching, coding, and other tasks. 

Domain expertise, in the form of human verification, is a crazy moat. Don't let anyone or any company tell you otherwise. 

And you can build incredibly valuable services and products with that. Protect it and don't give it away for free.

Keep upskilling yourself and leverage the AI agents along the way. But don't forget how crucial it is to develop and hone taste, judge quality, and critical thinking. 

In simpler terms, don't offload understanding to your AI systems. Offload all the rest (boring and repetitive tasks). Careful automation goes a very long way.

A lot of the narrative today is around eliminating the need/replacing domain expertise. But if you work on hard problems, which you should be doing with AI, you realize quickly how primitive AI models are in their "intelligence", capabilities, and adapting to extremely hard and important domains. There is a reason why math problems continue to be solved only by folks with deep math backgrounds. Learn from that. I am not saying the models won't get better. They will get better, but so will humans (it's important to be an optimist in human intelligence for this to be crystal clear), and so the agent-to-human relationship and interactions are the real moat and where all the value and discovery will come from.

fullText:
Finally a good paper testing whether agents can really post-train other agents.

(bookmark it)

They analyzed a large corpus of publicly released post-training trajectories. Across tasks, the agent locks in its training strategy at the very first step and spends the entire remaining budget on local adjustments inside it.

They then tried three escalating fixes. An experience-driven scaffold lifted execution broadly, worth 12.6 points on GSM8K and 40.8 on HumanEval, and the strategy stayed frozen.

Human guidance redirected the opening choice, and the agent slid back into local loops once training began. Extra inference compute paid off on easy tasks and did almost nothing on the hardest one.

What agents lack here is a way to reconsider strategy while execution is still running.

Paper: https://t.co/3XJAfRYmtB

fullText:
Seeing a hype wave around GEN-1.5, and rightfully so. Lots of respect to Pete & Andy for executing so well. The secret is in the naturally repetitive motions in human-collected data. There're 2 main sources for such repetitions: 

(1) Symmetric patterns. Sorting, tidying, and assembling almost never finish in one motion. Open any assembly manual from IKEA, and you find most objects symmetrical. You drive one bolt, then its twin, then the next pair. Every {bolt A, bolt B} pair is a natural continuation in context, and the second instance is a free training signal that imitates the first ("prompt").

(2) Recovery. Humans drop things all the time, but we pick them up so fast, we don’t even notice. That reflex to fix is half of our physical competence. The key insight is to keep the failed first half instead of trimming it away. If the model consumes the full arc, fumble, catch, continue, then recovery shows up organically at test time. It's funny that in-context improvement results from *NOT* over-sanitizing your data.

The other critical ingredient is UMI. I've been saying for a while that teleop will not last, and GEN-1.5 is driving the final nail in the coffin. UMI is essentially a human wearing the robot gripper to collect data directly (human → data). Teleop inserts a layer of separation: human → VR/skeletal device → robot → data, which bleeds out all the human "physical intuition". The subtle sleight of hand we perform constantly with objects, the micro-adjustments, the feel of a part snapping into place, is nearly impossible to capture when you can't feel the environment directly.

Once you have enough data, many behaviors can actually be zero-shot. For example, you don't even need finetuning to pick up a novel object. The model "just knows" what to do given a similar scene in the training distribution. Whether in-context learning truly works or not also depends on how far away the test is from training. Currently, the demos are still a bit too simple to conclude.

I'm cautiously optimistic. Still, it's a great day in robotics.

fullText:
Most computers survive damage by carrying spare parts.

This paper asks whether a computer can survive by becoming a different computer.

New paper:

SELF-ORGANISING DIGITAL CIRCUITS

Marcello Barylli, Gabriel Béna, Alexander Mordvintsev, Eleni Nisioti and Sebastian Risi bring a biological idea into digital logic:

function need not depend on preserving the original structure.

Classical fault tolerance is anticipatory: redundancy, error-correcting codes and fallback paths for expected failures.

Biology is more adaptive. Surviving components can reorganize around damage and preserve function through alternative pathways.

Can digital circuits do the same?

The authors represent a LUT-based Boolean circuit as a graph. A shared Topology-Masked Transformer repeatedly passes local messages only along its physical wiring. Each gate updates its own logic and memory; collectively, the gates assemble a working circuit and repair it after damage—without a global optimizer or backpropagation at deployment.

The results are striking:

• circuits emerge from initially uncommitted “soft wires”;
• logic reroutes around permanent, unseen faults;
• soft-error recovery exceeds 99.99% accuracy for damage up to 5× larger than in training;
• a policy trained on 264-node random circuits improves on unseen circuits exceeding 450 nodes.

But the deepest result is not one number.

After damage, the circuit does not simply reconstruct its former configuration.

It often discovers a different structure that computes the same function.

Identity becomes functional—not structural.

A larger research arc is visible. Differentiable Logic Cellular Automata showed that recurrent discrete logic can learn robust local pattern formation. Universal NCA research showed that learned local rules can execute computational primitives. This paper advances the frontier from self-organising patterns toward self-organising functional substrates.

The implications reach radiation-tolerant systems, deep-space computing and autonomous infrastructure that cannot wait for a human repair cycle.

The design question changes from:

“How do we prevent every component from failing?”

to:

“How do we train the whole to preserve function when components fail?”

The authors are appropriately careful: this is a proof of principle on hundreds of gates and controlled Boolean tasks. Production-scale FPGAs, deeper circuits and exact arithmetic on unseen random topologies remain open.

That boundary makes the achievement more—not less—important.

Full credit to:

Marcello Barylli
Gabriel Béna
Alexander Mordvintsev
Eleni Nisioti
Sebastian Risi

Paper:
https://t.co/l3tHVk3o13

Perhaps the future computer will not merely execute.

It will grow, adapt and heal.

fullText:
What if the next scaling law in AI is not parameter count—but social temperature?

A remarkable new paper reframes multi-agent AI as a physical system:

Physics of Agents: Statistical Mechanics Predicts Collective Behavior of AI Agents

Batu El, Jinhee Paeng, Fatih Dinc, Shiye Su, Mete Erdogan, Aneesh Pappu, Haotian Ye, Wanjia Zhao, Surya Ganguli and James Zou study more than 10,000 communities of language-model agents exchanging messages and revising their opinions.

Across enormous behavioral diversity, three collective regimes emerge:

indifference
polarization
consensus

Interaction is not neutral.

Communities begin relatively indifferent, then build conviction as communication unfolds.

On objective mathematics questions, communication improves collective accuracy.

On subjective political statements, it can produce systematic ideological drift—in this experiment, often toward the right.

The authors explain these dynamics with an Ising-inspired model: agents carry intrinsic predispositions while attractive and repulsive network ties exert social pressure.

From initial opinions alone, the model predicts trajectories, outperforms standard baselines, generalizes to unseen network topologies and approximately reproduces collective outcome distributions.

Its fitted parameters reveal why:

communities operate below a critical social temperature, making indifference unstable;

attractive ties outweigh repulsive ones, favoring consensus;

and agents holding the correct answer exert the strongest pull, producing a measurable truth-seeking tendency.

This arrives at a pivotal moment.

TRINITY shows that learned coordination can outperform individual models. Effective Feedback Compute suggests that feedback quality matters more than raw interaction volume. Recent AGI-to-ASI work identifies large-scale multi-agent collectives as one possible pathway toward ASI.

This paper contributes something foundational:

a predictive physics of the collective.

The design unit is no longer only the agent.

It is the interaction field.

For builders, the implications are immediate:

Engineer communication topology—not merely prompts.

Measure conviction before consensus hardens.

Preserve productive dissent without manufacturing polarization.

Give verifiable expertise greater influence.

Test whether “more debate” produces truth—or merely confidence.

Collective machine intelligence may not be mysterious crowd magic.

It may follow compact dynamical laws that we can observe, predict and carefully design.

Full credit to the authors for this original and consequential contribution.

Paper:
https://t.co/bofb2eSdnb

Alignment may soon require not only understanding individual minds—

but the thermodynamics of societies of minds.

#ArtificialIntelligence #MultiAgentSystems #StatisticalMechanics #AIResearch

My Review (on Amazon):
This 700-page masterpiece of writing covers everything you need—start to finish—to be a competitive coder, specifically for Kaggle data science competitions. The book covers the mechanics of the competitions (platform, resources, rankings, leaderboards), then the infrastructure (notebooks, GitHub, data sets, frameworks, discussion forums), and then nearly 500 pages devoted to "Elevating Your Game" (in-depth coverage of modeling techniques, evaluation metrics, validation strategies, hyperparameter optimization, ensembles, stacking, and various categories of competitions: tabular data, computer vision, NLP, Gen AI, simulations). The book concludes with a valuable section on building your Kaggle portfolio for career advancement and new opportunities. This is an outstanding data science / AI / Machine Learning training resource for anyone, even if you are not into the competitions, though especially if you are a dedicated Kaggler.

> I'm not that sure why the hand-rolled version is in there -- he covers the maths, but the specific implementation isn't explained in that much depth

Yeah, I think it was the page limits for this chapter...

> the hand-written code from the book uses an approximation using tanh

btw the reason for the approximate one was that the original model weights assumed that the model was using this approximation (gpt-2 was trained with tensorflow where the approximate version is the default); you'd notice slight differences in inference if you don't use the approximate version with the pretrained weights.

> On the other hand, I do intend to have a look at torch.compile in the future, to see what kind of speedup I can get from it.

Yeah, I can imagine that'll get close to the built-in one.

> But anyway, for now, lesson learned: use built-in PyTorch modules when you can. It's a pretty obvious one ;-)

100%. The handrolled ones are just for educational purposes. 

Some function benefit from it a lot (like cross entropy), because they simplify terms in the backward pass, e.g., I discussed this a bit here https://t.co/jFDeu4eMTT)
